articles.text: Police Department to move some activities to Piedmont Center for the Arts Walk-in services at the Piedmont Police Department (PPD) will be temporarily limited beginning in June. During this time, services at the Police Station will be reconfigured to accommodate the construction of the department’s new dispatch center project. With the reception area under construction, visitor accommodations similar to those used during COVID-19, will be implemented. Commonly requested forms will be available outside the building, and a phone will be installed outside to connect visitors with police staff inside. During construction, the offices that were previously used for evidence processing, officer report writing, and briefings will be converted into an interim dispatch center. Police have been working with the Public Works Department and city IT staff for several months to rewire and retrofit the facility to ensure that service is uninterrupted during this transition period. With the Police Department’s floor space reduced by 32%, the department will relocate some of its functions to the “flex space” in the Center for the Arts building at 801 Magnolia Avenue. articles.text: In the most recent school board meeting, May 8, teachers union President Elise Marks used the bulk of her allotted time to give an update on the contract negotiation impasse with the district. Marks and the Association of Piedmont Teachers (APT) informed Superintendent Jennifer Hawn and the school board that they really need to come to an agreement by Monday, May 20, in order to ratify it this school year. Classified CSEA workers of the district recently secured a contract with a similar raise structure to what Piedmont School District has offered teachers. Salary raises of 2.5 % this year, 4% next year and 3% for 2025-2026 were accepted in April. The district’s smallest labor group, the Association of Piedmont School Administrators (APSA), has around 20 employees, and includes Principals and Asst. Principals. APSA also came to an agreement with the school district with similar raise amounts during the May 8 board meeting, leaving only the teachers without new contracts. articles.text: The writers of the Christian scriptures understood that their intended audience was likely to be very familiar with the stories, songs and admonitions of the Hebrew Bible. This is certainly true for the writer of the Gospel of Luke and its sequel, the Book of Acts. We see this in Acts chapter two as Luke tells the story of the Day of Pentecost. Pentecost originated as an agricultural festival, but by the time of Jesus it would also have been a covenant renewal ceremony celebrating the giving of Torah at Mount Sinai. Working with this background, Luke makes it clear that the gift of the Holy Spirit on Pentecost is akin to the gift of the Torah on the mountain as the people began their wilderness sojourn after escaping Egypt. On Mt. Sinai there was wind, fire and a voice, all representing God’s presence. On that Pentecost Sunday in Jerusalem, there was the rush of a mighty wind, tongues of fire descending on the heads of the disciples and voices of people of the many nations that had gathered in the Holy City, all representing the powerful manifestation of God’s Spirit. Fire was central to the theophany on Mt. Sinai. Fire was central to the theophany of Pentecost. I like what Baptist prophet Ken Sehested says about the fire of Pentecost. “The flame of the Spirit’s igniting presence does not scorch us. It makes us radiant.” Fire is both essential for life and a threat to life. Without the fire of the sun, we could not survive on planet earth. The coming of yet another fire season reminds us that fire is a clear and present danger. Fire can certainly scorch and scar us. articles.text: Cyclists from Piedmont and across the Bay Area will mount their bicycles tomorrow and ride off to work and school in the Bay Area’s 30th annual Bike to Wherever Day on Thursday, May 16. An energizer station at Highland and Vista Avenues will dispense coffee and other refreshments to riders courtesy of Mulberry’s Market from 7 to 9 a.m. The station will be set up by the City of Piedmont’s Sustainability Division. Riders may also stop by for a free tote bag while supplies last, and a raffle entry to win a bicycle cleaning kit. Bike to Wherever Day was founded in 1994 to celebrate bicycles as a healthy way to get to work. Originally called “Bike to Work Day,” the event was renamed during the pandemic to encourage people to ride their bikes for other occasions as well, including running errands or meeting their friends. With transportation accounting for almost half of Piedmont’s total greenhouse gas emissions, encouraging more residents to use greener commute options is vital to meeting the City’s Climate Action targets. The event is organized each year by Bike East Bay, a nonprofit organization based in Oakland. • Events for the public include: • Bike to School Day: Every year the Safe Routes to • • Schools Program in Alameda County joins the Bay Area region in celebrating May as Bike Month with the biggest celebration on Bike to School Day. Oakland Group Ride with Elected Officials: (7 a.m. - 8:30 a.m.) Join Mayor of Oakland Sheng Thao and members of Oakland City Council for a ride through the city. Riders will meet at various locations in the city before meeting at Frank Ogawa Plaza at 8:30 a.m. and then riding to Oakland City Hall. See website for details. Berkeley Group Ride with Elected Officials: (8:15 a.m.) Join members of Berkeley City Council for a ride through town. Riders will meet at the North Berkeley BART station and ride to Berkeley City Hall. Bike Happy Hour: (4 p.m. - 8 p.m.) Celebrate the Bike Day in the streets of l Old Oakland at Washington and 10th Street. PPD Support Services Commander Lisa Douglas stated that the space will be used “daily but for short periods” as needed until construction is complete. The impacts are significant for Piedmont Police who currently are working out of a space 40-50% smaller than those of similarly-sized agencies in the East Bay. “I’m not sure how comfortable [our officers] are going to be in a building that’s not the police department, but we just don’t have any other space here to do those types of things during construction,” Douglas explained. “I’m sure that as things move along in this construction process, we’ll learn what works and what doesn’t and we’ll adjust accordingly,” stated Douglas. Douglas also confirmed that the department has no plans to relocate any “heavy equipment” to 801 Magnolia Avenue and that the area will not be for dispatch use. Police Chief Jeremy Bowers has shared his appreciation to the community for their patience and support. “As the Police Department prepares for the Dispatch Center upgrade, we are mindful of the disruption the construction will cause to our working environment and to visitors. articles.text: Piedmont Scout Council’s annual Bike Rodeo drew a large number of kids to the playground at Beach School last Saturday, May 11. Beginning at 9:00 a.m. local youth gathered on their bikes to negotiate a detailed traffic course in multicolored chalk designed to teach children safe rules of the road. In addition to the traffic course, a variety of different stations had activities aimed at getting youth excited to use their bikes during the summer, including a trivia wheel, a station testing riders’ braking abilities, and a new crowd favorite. a pedal-powered, smoothie-making Bike Blender. “We had a lot more kids this year, which was great,” said Eris Turner, the Council’s Program Coordinator. “We’re always looking to get more word out and keep it going. The kids enjoy biking, and it’s a lot of fun to put on.” The obstacle course, the undisputed main event of the Bike Rodeo, has grown in complexity in comparison to previous years. The course had several roundabouts, four-way intersections with stop signs, and yield signs. Obstacles were color-coded for clarity, and signs were drawn on the ground in chalk. Police Explorers from Piedmont’s Post #911 also ran a station designed to test riders’ abilities to stop on a dime. The Explorers set up a strip where youth could build up speed and test how fast they could go, even using a radar gun. Then, riders were challenged to stop within 10 feet of a given target. “We made sure to run it on an uphill so they couldn’t get too crazy there,” laughed Turner. Piedmont Police Officer Tyler Petit and Community Service Officers Haley Shedd and Nancy Flores were also present to supervise the Explorers. However, the activity that stole the show was the Bike Blender – a clever invention donated by one of the rodeo’s partners, Alameda County Safe Routes to School. The Bike Blender is a stationary bicycle whose back wheels are hooked up to a blender by way of a specially fitted gear. By pedaling the bike, eventgoers could make their own smoothies with materials provided by the Scout Council. In a surprise to organizers, children tended to use healthier ingredients like mixed fruits, bananas, milk, yogurt, and peanut butter over the provided ice cream. Westside Joe’s Bicycle Shop of Alameda could not make it to the event as planned, so Cycles of Change, an East Bay nonprofit organization, was on hand to help young riders with their safety checks, including things like making sure riders had helmets and that riders knew how to operate their gear shifts properly. The event was hosted in partnership with Alameda County Safe Routes to School, a program that organizes and supports fun, educational activities encouraging families to walk, bike, carpool, and take transit to school.

We believe we are so close to agreement that waiting until late May or June for Fact-Finding – and therefore going into summer without a deal – will only cause more teachers with outside offers to make the choice to leave. To prevent any further loss of great educators, APT asks district leadership to agree with us mutually to formally end Impasse and make our most recent offers open to the public. Ending Impasse would also take the threat of a strike off the table, and lessen the anxiety the community has felt about that possibility. APT believes that if the community understands what’s holding us back from a deal, they will agree with APT’s position and see our path forward very clearly. APT is here and ready to talk at any time. We are asking the members of the School Board to please take that final step and reach an agreement.

articles.text: This month, observers in Nor ther n Califor nia were treated to a rare and dazzling display of colorful lights. These radiant lights, commonly known as the Northern Lights or aurora borealis, became visible in areas of the Bay Area due to a recent and intense geomagnetic storm. What triggered the geomagnetic storm? Multiple Coronal Mass Ejections (CMEs), which are large explosions of plasma and magnetic field from the Sun’s atmosphere. At least four of these CMEs sent clouds of charged particles in the direction of Earth. As these particles interacted with the Earth’s magnetic field, they were deflected towards the magnetics poles, entering the atmosphere and producing auroras. Did you know? Due to the intensity of the storms, there was also a chance of disturbance in the Earth’s magnetic field, which may have resulted in communication disruptions and possibly power failures in the days that followed. A stellar sight to see Reflecting on this awe-inspiring weekend, we’re reminded of the beauty and power of Mother Nature. We’re not sure when we’ll have another chance to see the Northern Lights again in the Bay Area, but we invite you to join us for our free public telescope viewing events every Friday and Saturday from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., weather permitting. articles.text: Fundraising concert held at Oakland Zoo in April Grateful Dead founding member Bob Weir is the latest celebrity to support one of Oakland’s hidden gems, Northern Light School, an independent progressive school in Oakland, dedicated to serving children from all socioeconomic backgrounds in grades pre-K to 8th. On April 19, Weir played an intimate benefit concert for Northern Light School. Past star supporters have included Bonnie Raitt, Peter Coyote, Jackson Browne, MC Hammer, and baseball star Vida Blue. At Northern Light School, 75 percent of students receive tuition assistance, compared to the national average for independent schools of less than 25 percent. 95 percent of NLS’ students are children of color, compared to the national average of 34 percent. Remaining steadfast to the school mission means a lot of fundraising for a small entity like Northern Light. Like other independent schools, NLS has experienced budgetary challenges coming out of the pandemic due to increased rent and salary costs to keep up with the ever-rising Bay Area cost of living. “We’re so grateful that Bobby did this for us,” said NLS Head of School Sanjev deSilva. “Times are tough and he totally came through.” The fundraiser was held in partnership with the Oakland Zoo, where Oakland Zoo CEO Nik Dehejia kicked off the evening with welcoming remarks, and guests got to walk through flamingo, tiger and giraffe exhibits on their way to the concert venue. A surprise moment of the evening was when one of Northern Light’s four founders, Michelle Lewis, announced that she would be donating her salary back to the school. “It’s for the children,” she said. “Anything for the children. When the founders and I opened the school in 1989, we wanted it to be for children from all walks of life, even if they couldn’t pay. It means so much to me that this same dream continues today.” Northern Light School prioritizes academic excellence as well as non-violence, acceptance of differences, respect for the environment and the moral advancement of humanity so that children develop an understanding that they have a responsibility to make a difference in the lives of others. The school boasts unique program offerings like an annual 8th grade trip to Washington, DC to learn about the importance of civic duty; and a biweekly Morning Circle to affirm the community’s values by discussing world events, celebrating important days, honoring cultural heritage, and hosting diverse speakers and performers. Over 90 percent of graduating 8th graders matriculate to private or parochial high schools and the same percentage attend and graduate from college. “Our annual benefit concert was a really big deal and affirmed all the love that Northern Light School supporters have at this time. Bobby Weir was a big part of that,” said deSilva. For more information contact the school by e-mail at: boardchair@nlsoakland.com

articles.text: Tonight, May 15, the American Medical Women’s Association, Highlander Robotics FRC Team 8033 and Girl Scouts Service Unit 303 will present a special screening of the Paramount Plus award-winning film, Afghan Dreamers. Afghan Dreamers tells the incredible story of the Afghan Dreamers Girls’ Robotics Team, a group of Afghan schoolgirls who – led and inspired by Afghan tech entrepreneur Roya Mahboob – defied conservative gender roles to compete internationally in robotics. In doing so, they helped transform a people and nation. The team first gained international notice in 2017 when they were barred from attending FIRST Global in Washington, D.C., due to a travel ban against individuals from certain predominantly Muslim countries. Supported by international allies and with the intervention of members of Congress, the team was ultimately allowed to compete and went on to win several awards in the U.S. and internationally. Inspired by the Dreamers’ unlikely success, then-President Ashraf Ghani committed to building five STEM schools throughout Afghanistan. But the team’s journey came with many struggles, as the film poignantly demonstrates. The Dreamers then continued their international journey, transforming communities and bringing hope to women and girls along the way. But, as the film painfully shows, a tragic reversal of fortune came in August 2018 when the Taliban gained control of Afghanistan, and the girls, their coaches, and thousands of other Afghans were forced to flee their homeland. This film has special relevance to the Bay Area, as the Dreamers spent over a week in Piedmont hosted by a local family through the American Medical Women’s Association. During this time, the team had the opportunity to spend time with Piedmont robotics teams, Girl Scouts, and Boy Scouts. “Opening our home to the team was one of those unique moments in life that transforms the way you view and embrace the world and forges special friendships that last a lifetime,” said Douglas and Eliza Chin. Immediately following the screening on May 15, members of the production team will be joined by a former Afghan Dreamers team captain as well as an Afghan Girl Scout. They will share their perspectives on the film and the current status of women’s rights in Afghanistan, particularly with regard to education and work. The discussion will be moderated by an Afghan writer and human rights activist. The film has received critical acclaim internationally, awarded Best Human Rights Documentary at the Galway Film Fleadh, Runner-Up for Best Feature Length Documentary at Woodstock, Audience Choice Award at the Valladolid International Film Festival and Official Selection at the Heartland and Boulder International Film Festivals.

pages.text: Wednesday, May 15, 2024 9 PHS students place 3rd in UC Berkeley Bioengineering competition Piedmont High School students Josephine Oesterer (left), Jamie Schwarz, Jeremy Tuan, Mark Hsia and Miles Antaya competed in the event for the second time and placed 3rd this year. By Shelley Seto-Rosen On Saturday, April 6, three teams of Piedmont High School (PHS) students competed in the BioEHSC, an annual high school bioengineering competition run by the UC Berkeley Bioengineering Honor Society. PHS competed against 50 national and California teams including entries from top schools from across the Bay Area. The Piedmont team of seniors Josephine Oesterer, Jamie Schwarz, Jeremy Tuan, Mark Hsia and Miles Antaya earned a second place finish in last year’s competition. Their project this year earned a third-place finish in a very competitive field. Theirs was the only complete PHS team to compete in multiple years and is the school’s most successful team to date. The BioEHSC is a research and design competition in which teams define a biological problem, complete research, and then propose a novel engineering solution to the problem. The teams were sponsored by AP Biology teacher Shelley SetoRosen and were each matched with a UC Berkeley Bioengineering mentor. Seven weeks of preparation culminated in an in-person competition on the UC Berkeley campus. Projects were judged on a video submission, a poster session, an academic presentation, and an industry (water cooler) pitch. PHS projects entered in BioEHSC • • Electric Stimulation of Arbuscular Mycorrhizal Fungi to Increase Mycelia-Plant Mutualism By Josephine Oesterer, Jamie Schwarz, Jeremy Tuan, Mark Hsia and Miles Antaya “We propose a novel device that electrically stimulates the germination and growth of Arbuscular Mycorrhizal Fungi. A grid of modules containing spores, electrodes, and growth promoting matter create a network of mycelium with mutualistic relationships with crops, reducing fertilizer costs and environmental impact while increasing crop yield and arable land,” explained senior Mark Hsia. Creating Accessible Treatment for Erythrodermic Psoriasis with a Transdermal Microneedle Methotrexate (TdMnM) Patch By Genevieve Hiller, Logan Watral, Aman Jajodia, Inaya Majid and Emmett Baldwin. “We created a transdermal microneedle patch to treat • erythrodermic psoriasis, a rarer but more severe and potentially fatal form of psoriasis. We created an accessible microneedle patch using the drug methotrexate, which inhibits the buildup of t-cells in the dermal layer which causes the scaly plaque-like formations on the skin associated with psoriasis. It is an effective and affordable option that can significantly increase accessibility to quality treatment for the millions affected by psoriasis globally,” said junior Aman Jajodia Idebenone Eye Drops as a Novel Treatment for Open Angle Glaucoma By Anne Reardon, Ayaan Jajodia, Beck Peterson, Elsa Rivera and Maeve Gaylord “Glaucoma, affecting approximately 60 million people, is the second leading cause of blindness globally and is characterized by an increase in intraocular pressure resulting in the death of retinal ganglion cells. Our proposed treatment, eye drops with Idebenone and prostaglandin analogs, offers a safer and more effective treatment than other glaucoma medications by inhibiting an early enzyme of the TGF-β pathway, stopping glaucoma at its root cause,” explained senior Anne Reardon. PHS participants in the UC Berkeley bioengineering competition included Ayaan Jajodia (left), Maeve Gaylord, Beck Peterson, Ann Reardon, Mark Hsia, Jamie Schwarz, Josephine Oesterer, Jeremy Tuan, Genevieve Hiller, Emmett Baldwin, Logan Watral, Aman Jajodia and Inaya Majid. Afghan Dreamers film at Driscoll Playhouse tonight Tonight, May 15, the American Medical Women’s Association, Highlander Robotics FRC Team 8033 and Girl Scouts Service Unit 303 will present a special screening of the Paramount Plus award-winning film, Afghan Dreamers. Afghan Dreamers tells the incredible story of the Afghan Dreamers Girls’ Robotics Team, a group of Afghan schoolgirls who – led and inspired by Afghan tech entrepreneur Roya Mahboob – defied conservative gender roles to compete internationally in robotics. In doing so, they helped transform a people and nation. The team first gained international notice in 2017 when they were barred from attending FIRST Global in Washington, D.C., due to a travel ban against individuals from certain predominantly Muslim countries. Supported by international allies and with the intervention of members of Congress, the team was ultimately allowed to compete and went on to win several awards in the U.S. and internationally. Inspired by the Dreamers’ unlikely success, then-President Ashraf Ghani committed to building five STEM schools throughout Afghanistan. But the team’s journey came with many struggles, as the film poignantly demonstrates. The Dreamers then continued their international journey, transforming communities and bringing hope to women and girls along the way. But, as the film painfully shows, a tragic reversal of fortune came in August 2018 when the Taliban gained control of Afghanistan, and the girls, their coaches, and thousands of other Afghans were forced to flee their homeland. This film has special relevance to the Bay Area, as the Dreamers spent over a week in Piedmont hosted by a local family through the American Medical Women’s Association. During this time, the team had the opportunity to spend time with Piedmont robotics teams, Girl Scouts, and Boy Scouts. “Opening our home to the team was one of those unique moments in life that transforms the way you view and embrace the world and forges special friendships that last a lifetime,” said Douglas and Eliza Chin. Immediately following the screening on May 15, members of the production team will be joined by a former Afghan Dreamers team captain as well as an Afghan Girl Scout. They will share their perspectives on the film and the current status of women’s rights in Afghanistan, particularly with regard to education and work. The discussion will be moderated by an Afghan writer and human rights activist. The film has received critical acclaim internationally, awarded Best Human Rights Documentary at the Galway Film Fleadh, Runner-Up for Best Feature Length Documentary at Woodstock, Audience Choice Award at the Valladolid International Film Festival and Official Selection at the Heartland and Boulder International Film Festivals. The morning started with opening assemblies and period 1 teachers leading discussions about the speakers they would hear and their areas of expertise or experience. This reporter first ventured to Diversity Day newcomer Sandi Hunt who was teaching a “foraging and wildcrafting” lesson on a little dirt hill bordering the school’s Magnolia Avenue side. Hunt brought various herbs and woodland discoveries to show students some of the many uses of plants with hopes of students becoming mindful stewards of the planet. articles.text: Piedmont High’s track and field team had terrific results at this year’s North Coast Section Bayshore Championship on Saturday, May 11 at James Logan HS in Union City, resulting in 13 top-six finishes to automatically qualify for the NCS Meet of Champions at Dublin High School on Friday and Saturday, May 17-18. The Highlanders also gained two more At-Large bids for the Meet of Champions, giving them 19 athletes spread across 15 events at next week’s prestigious meet. PHS athletes will now have a chance to qualify for the CIF State Championship on May Photos by Becky Spies Breah Bell qualified in two individual events for the NCS Meet of Champions and is also runs the anchor leg on the 4x100 relay team that qualified. Ella Yasar was third in the 300 hurdles and helped the 4x400 team qualify for the NCS Meet of Champions. Freshman Sebastien Swain will compete in the 1600 meters at the Meet of Champions. 24-25 at Buchanan High School in Clovis. The top three in each event will automatically qualify for State. “In the end every athlete we had hoped to get through to the NCS Meet of Champs got through, plus more. That’s about as good as it gets,” said coach Pouyan Assadi, “While we didn’t take 1st in any events this year our depth was on display as we’re sending the most athletes to MOC in school history.” It marked another stellar performance by senior Breah Bell, who qualified in two individual events plus the relays. Bell finished fourth of 23 sprinters in the 100-meter sprint with a personal record time of 12.55 seconds. She also claimed an At-Large bid in the long jump, finishing ninth of 22 with a distance of 16 feet, 7.5 inches. Bell ran the anchor leg of the 4x100 relay team, which included Miranda Liu, Ella Yasar, and Claire Aubrecht. Their team was fourth of 20 teams with a time of 50.03. According to school records on Athletic.net, Bell’s time in the 100 broke Toni Ali Daggao’s 100-meters record of 12.91 in 2017. “Our girls captains were the stars of the show, with Breah breaking the Piedmont 100m record. It’s nice having a group that’s so dependable,” Assadi said. Senior Jamie Schwarz qualified in the 800 meters, finishing fourth of 22 with a time of 2:23.24. She narrowly missed out on qualifying in the 1600, where she was seventh in 5:21.26. Schwarz also ran the third leg of the 4x400 relay team that was fourth with a time of 4:15.44. Schwarz ran with Daniela Lucaccini as first leg, Skylar Best as the second, and Yasar as anchor. Yasar had an impressive thirdplace run in the 300 meter hurdles in a field of 24 athletes, clocking a time of 48.47. Best also gained an At-Large big in the 1600 with a time of 5:26.81, finishing eighth of 22. The girls’ 4x800 team of Ryo Woltag, Caroline Taylor, Gladwin Horsely, and Nasreen Schulze had a big performance, finishing second of 13 with a time of 10:26.07.

The baseball team, seeded No. 2, will host the winner of No. 7 Fort Bragg vs. No. 10 Hercules on Saturday, May 18. The softball team with a No. 5 seed will play at No. 4 Fortuna on Saturday. BASEBALL Piedmont’s baseball team enters NCS with a 15-8 overall record and the Bo. 2 seed. After finishing the regular season in first-place of the Western Alameda County Conference Foothill Division, they faltered in an extra-inning battle to Alameda in the WACC Tournament semifinals, and lost 4-3. They are looking ahead to No. 7 Fort Bragg or No. 10 Hercules. PHS didn’t have any common opponents with Fort Bragg this year. As for Hercules, both Piedmont and the Titans faced Justin-Siena this season. PHS beat the Braves 1-0, but Hercules got demolished 17-0. The Highlanders enter post-season with one of its most complete lineups in coach Eric Olson’s career. Markos Lagios is hitting at a .372 clip, has a team-leading six home runs, 27 runs scored, 25 RBIs, 29 hits, and six stolen bases. He was recently named the Foothill Division’s Most Valuable Player. Piedmont also has options on the mound. John Olsen has been stellar with a 2.43 ERA over 40.1 innings of work with 40 strikeouts and two saves. Seve Sanchez has also been strong with a 1.34 ERA over 26 innings and 24 strikeouts. Peter Krumins, who slots in at shortstop, is also a force on the mound with 20.2 innings pitched with 25 strikeouts, and a 3.04 ERA. SOFTBALL The Highlanders walk into the NCS postseason with a 10-7 overall record and went 6-5 in the WACC’s Shoreline Division. They received a first-round bye in NCS as the No. 5 seed and are scheduled to face No. 4 Fortuna in the Quarterfinals on May 18. The NCS office elected to give the top six teams in the D4 playoffs a first-round bye, while the bottom four seeds play on May 15 to face No. 1 St. Helena and No. 2 Del Norte. Piedmont will travel five hours to Fortuna in Northern California for its Saturday meeting. articles.text: Stern Grove Festival audiences enjoy free concerts. Stern Grove Festival, the country’s oldest nonprofit and free music festival, kicks off on June 23. Headliners this year are electronic duo Sylvan Esso and iconic funk superstar Chaka Khan. The amphitheater at Sigmund Stern Grove in San Francisco will host ten weeks of admission-free concerts beginning June 23 and running through August 25. Reservation is required and is given on a first-come, first-serve basis. Last year’s festival drew 90,000 attendees over the course of two months. The festival, now in its 87th season, opens June 23 with performances by King Isis, a queer Oakland-based multi-genre artist, and sibling pop duo Tegan and Sara. San Francisco Symphony will perform a special concert on July 7 with Jessica Vosk, who performed as Elphaba in the Broadway musical Wicked. The SFJazz Collective, an all-star ensemble, will partner with jazz pianist Herbie Hancock for an August 11 performance. The Big Picnic Weekend, the festival’s annual fundraiser, is expanding this year to two days. Stern Grove Festival Association is a non-profit organization whose mission is “to make live musical experiences accessible to all.” Since its inception in 1938, the organization has presented the free concert series “Stern Grove Festival” in Sigmund Stern Grove, an outdoor amphitheater located at 19th Avenue and Sloat Boulevard in San Francisco. The amphitheater is owned and operated by the City of San Francisco. The natural amphitheater is surrounded by giant eucalyptus, redwood, and fir trees and has become the home of one of Northern California’s most well-attended summer concert sites. The festival has brought to the public more than eight decades of performing arts, including opera, theater, and music. mer performances. Visit https:// www.sterngrove.org to reserve tickets.

articles.text: Circadian String Quartet performs its first concert at Piedmont Center for the Arts on Friday, May 24 at 7:30 pm. Titled Love and Chains, the concert includes special guests Leslie Bonnet and Nikolaus Hohmann. Tickets are $25 general/$15 seniors and students and are available at www.eventbrite. com/e/894985956087. The concert explores the deep bonds and binds that come with Love. Experience the world premiere of an original chamber opera, Euridice’s Defiance, composed by David Ryther. Inspired by the Greek myth of Orpheus and Euridice, this work in progress tells the story of a mother, Euridice, being detained at a border crossing and separated from her son, Orpheus, while she pleads with her guard to re-unite them. The ground-breaking libretto, written by novelist Kimiko Guthrie, is set to a haunting score by Ryther. The concert will also include Preludes by Claude Debussy, arranged for string quartet; Anton Webern’s romantic opus Langsamer Satz, and two works by Iranian-born composer Sahba Aminikia which are profound meditations on geopolitical struggles that are born from the love of our common humanity.

In this retelling, Galileo is summoned to Rome to defend his discoveries before the most powerful religious institution in the world. The play is accompanied with an original rock score with lyrics by Michael Weiner and Zoe Sarnak, and features fourtime Tony Award nominee Raúl Esparza. The cast includes Bradley Dean as Bishop Grasso, Jeremy Kushnier as Bishop Maffeo Barberini, Madalynn Mathews as Virginia Galilei and Christian Magby as Alessandro Tarantola. Post-show discussions will be held on May 24, May 30, and June 4 by members of Berkeley Rep’s artistic team. The play ends June 23. Less than an hour before the encore’s opening night performance on April 30, Osipova withdrew due to an injury. The news was delivered from the stage by Tamara Rojo herself. After collective sighs of disappointment, Ms. Rojo announced that the role of Odette-Odile would be performed by Jasmine Jimison, a newly promoted principal dancer who would be making her debut in the role. Unsure of what to expect, the audience clapped politely. The lights dimmed, guest conductor Martin West raised his baton, and soon the theatre resounded with Tchaikovsky’s haunting music. As the curtain lifted to reveal an evening lake, I braced myself for rewatching something I had tried to forget. But the moment Jasmine Jimison appeared on the stage, I was smitten. With her clean lines and impeccable undulation of her arms that instantly reminded me of Maya Plisetskaya, Jimison seemed born for the role. As the story unfolded – Odette falling in love, Odile tricking her lover, Odette suffering from his unwitting betrayal – Jimison handled transitions between innocence and seduction, hope and despair with technical prowess and dramatic flair. Judging from the solid ovations and loud “Bravos” her numbers received, including the famous “Black Swan Coda” featuring 32 consecutive fouettés, I wasn’t the only person in the audience impressed with Jimison’s performance. Her strong delivery was particularly striking given the short notice of the cast change and the intense pressure Jimison, a Bay Area native, must have felt to perform in an international superstar’s stead. Not only did she have to turn around the audience’s disappointment, she also had to make her own mark in one of the ballet’s most demanding character roles. Jimison succeeded in both. I felt drawn into Odette’s tragic story like never before. As I watched Jimison-Odette love, hope, suffer, and ultimately ascend with her beloved (Jimison has a natural ability to develop character), I at last perceived Swan Lake not as a prelude to something bad like I had in my childhood, but as an enduring love story, a triumph of the spirit over death – and a testimony of human capacity to push the boundaries of the possible. Jimison didn’t do it alone, of course. Isaac Hernández as Prince Siegfried was a perfect match for Jimison’s Odette – poetic, ardent, and technically flawless. Impressing the audience with his clean, high, and effortless jumps, Hernández didn’t overpower the stage, achieving just the right balance between platonic love, passion, and sadness. Swan Lake is not an easy ballet for a male lead because of the built-in contradiction of the story: a hero who wows to save Odette, Siegfried fails to see the differences between her and Odile and professes his love to the wrong woman, forever ruining Odette’s chance to become human again. Paris-based Ballets Russes popularized Tchaikovsky’s masterpiece in Europe. In 1940, San Francisco Ballet introduced Swan Lake to American audiences. Judging from the solid ovations and loud “Bravos” her numbers received, including the famous “Black Swan Coda” featuring 32 consecutive fouettés, I wasn’t the only person in the audience impressed with Jimison’s performance. Her strong delivery was particularly striking given the short notice of the cast change and the intense pressure Jimison, a Bay Area native, must have felt to perform in an international superstar’s stead. Not only did she have to turn around the audience’s disappointment, she also had to make her own mark in one of the ballet’s most demanding character roles. Jimison succeeded in both. I felt drawn into Odette’s tragic story like never before. As I watched Jimison-Odette love, hope, suffer, and ultimately ascend with her beloved (Jimison has a natural ability to develop character), I at last perceived Swan Lake not as a prelude to something bad like I had in my childhood, but as an enduring love story, a triumph of the spirit over death – and a testimony of human capacity to push the boundaries of the possible. Jimison didn’t do it alone, of course. Isaac Hernández as Prince Siegfried was a perfect match for Jimison’s Odette – poetic, ardent, and technically flawless. Impressing the audience with his clean, high, and effortless jumps, Hernández didn’t overpower the stage, achieving just the right balance between platonic love, passion, and sadness. Swan Lake is not an easy ballet for a male lead because of the built-in contradiction of the story: a hero who wows to save Odette, Siegfried fails to see the differences between her and Odile and professes his love to the wrong woman, forever ruining Odette’s chance to become human again. For Siegfried not to lose the audience’s sympathy, Rothbart and Odile must act subtly. Luckily, Alexander Reneff-Olson as Von Rothbart was the perfect evil genius, believably outplaying the idealistic prince – in mortal life at least. Swan Lake is also one of the best ballets to showcase corps de ballet. The iconic second act requires at least three dozen swans on stage, all moving in perfect unison. In the SF Ballet’s encore production, the swan dancers were superb. Their white tutus and matching sparking headdresses provided a remarkable moonlit frame to Odette and Siegfried’s developing romance. The ethnic dances (Spanish, Czardas, Neapolitan and Russian) during the Act III imperial ball were delightful and sported bright national costumes designed by Jonathan Fensom. On the opening night, Fensom faced some serious competition from the audience members. I saw at least one man in an elaborate tiered swan costume complete with a headdress. The standing ovation that Jimison and her dance partners received at the final curtain confirmed the old adage: Fortune favors the brave. While it’s a joy to watch a ballet veteran deliver her predictably magnificent performances, there’s an undeniable thrill in witnessing the birth of a new star. On April 30th, Jimison’s command of the renowned stage was undeniable. As a fan of San Francisco Ballet, I can’t wait to see what Jasmine Jimison does next. She’s the author of Russia: Putin’s Playground, a concise guide to Russian politics, history, and culture.

articles.text: San Francisco’s iconic fog, affectionately dubbed “Karl” by us locals, adds a mystical allure to our cityscape. Known as advection fog, it drifts horizontally, shrouding the Golden Gate Bridge and steep hills in a dreamy mist. Formed when warm, moist air meets the cooler Pacific waters, it blankets our city, providing a natural air conditioner while fostering a romantic ambiance. Despite being foggiest from June through August, global warming means fewer and shorter foggy days. Nevertheless, Karl continues to envelop our city at his whim, as evidenced by the remarkable display we witnessed on April 11 from Marin Headlands. We embrace Karl’s presence for its contribution to our city’s unique charm and the mesmerizing beauty it lends to our photographs, further cementing our city’s well-deserved reputation as the City of Fog. These images were captured on Bay Area hikes in recent years, showcasing the stunning landscapes and natural beauty accentuated by Karl. These photos serve as a testament to the remarkable beauty of the Bay Area and the reason why I’ve chosen to call this place home for over 40 years. From misty trails to panoramic vistas, each photograph encapsulates the Bay Area’s unparalleled charm and the profound connection it fosters with nature. These images not only capture moments in time but also evoke my sense of gratitude for the privilege of experiencing such breathtaking scenery firsthand.

articles.text: Richard Gere and Ethan Hawke in Brooklyn’s Finest Cop movies are a time-tested genre. Some are referred to as police procedurals where an investigation is conducted in a rigorous, linear fashion. Others are, in essence, character studies, focusing on the exigencies of the job, the harshness of the environment, and the corruption of the human spirit. Many are hard-bitten morality plays, bringing into relief the universal struggle between good and evil. If done well, they can be superb entertainment. Examples are L.A. Confidential, Heat, To Live and Die in L.A., The French Connection, Se7en, Dirty Harry, Speed, Training Day, Die Hard, plus Roman Polanski’s Chinatown, one of the best. Brooklyn’s Finest focuses on three NYPD officers, Tango (Don Cheadle), Eddie (Richard Gere) and Sal (Ethan Hawke) who inhabit is the dark side of the city, riven with crime and drugs, where drugs and violence permeate. The film offers three snapshots of their lives as they move toward a fateful intersection. Each has made a Faustian bargain with some form of evil that will, in the end, spell ruin. Their journey makes for tense, gripping entertainment. There are moments in Brooklyn’s Finest when it seems all but necessary to suspend one’s disbelief so desperately raw and abysmal are the mean streets of Brooklyn. Is it possible that street cops are so deeply submerged in the inner city’s refuse that they begin to resemble the very people they are arresting? Friedrich Nietzche once wrote, “Whoever battles with monsters had better see that it does not turn him into a monster. And if you gaze long into the abyss, the abyss gazes also into you.” That is the admonition that haunts Brooklyn’s Finest. There’s Eddie, only seven days from retirement. He has long ago compromised himself and his oath to the point that he no longer cares. He is alone, his life so stark and sad that it has become devoid of purpose. In one scene he sits with the barrel of his revolver between his teeth. Tango, an undercover cop, lives each day with the violent exploitation of drug dealers and predators. People are disposable. All that matters is dope and money. Tango knows that he is lost, trapped in a labyrinth of destruction. His only wish is to get his life back and yet the universe conspires against him. Sal, a narcotics officer, is adrift, telling himself that the ends justify the means. His days are awash in druggies and drug money. Life is overwhelming him: he has children, a pregnant wife, a house that is moldy and hazardous and feels the pull of money as if it were an overwhelming gravity. Brooklyn’s Finest is a narrative that is intense and gritty. Some fans might call it pulp cinema, or a noirish tale that never flinches. This film will entertain and more. But be warned: it’s raw and violent and dark. Very dark. Brooklyn’s Finest. Directed by Antoine Fugua. Starring Richard Gere, Don Cheadle, Ethan Hawke, Wesley Snipes, Shannon Kane and Lili Taylor. 2 hrs., 5 min. Rated R. Now streaming on VUDU/prime/peacock/apple tv.

articles.text: A scene from Skydance Studio’s Luck Older kids, tweens, and newbie teens will enjoy watching the adventures of Sam Greenfield (Eva Nobelzada) in the animated feature film Luck. First some backstory about Sam: she’s a teenager who has aged out of her foster care family, and is sad to leave her younger friend Hazel (Adelyn Spoon) who is also an orphan waiting to be adopted by a family. Meanwhile, Sam has found a small apartment of her own and a job at a flower shop. As we come to know Sam better, we begin to understand that she feels alone, and is struggling to find her place in the world. But we also soon learn that Sam is resilient and optimistic, vivacious and considerate. What is making her life difficult on a daily basis is that she is plagued by bad luck. Put another way, some might say that Sam is a klutz. This is revealed through a number of funny scenes showing how she loses things, creates a mess wherever she goes, locks herself out of her bathroom, is often late for work, and even drops her morning toast, jam covered, face down. And so we find Sam sitting on a curb eating a sandwich, when a black cat comes and sits next to her and she offers it some of her Panini bread. Later she finds a penny that seems to unexpectedly bring her good luck. She decides to give the lucky penny to her friend Hazel. Perhaps it just might help her find that much sought after family. But true to form, Sam drops the penny into the toilet and once again bemoans her bad luck. Sam returns to her familiar curb and once again the black cat returns; however, when Sam tells the critter named Bob (Simon Pegg) about the penny he admonishes her in a surprising Scottish brogue, and tells her to follow him. He leads her through a portal, which reveals a magical place called the Land of Luck. Maybe there she might find that penny. And so Sam’s adventure begins in this extraordinary place filled with leprechauns led by The Captain (Whoopi Goldberg), an enormous pink dragon (Jane Fonda), and a unicorn named Jeff (Flula Borg). Sam learns a life lesson about luck that comes with insights and new realizations. Kids will enjoy Sam’s journey and all the characters she meets along the way. Luck. Directed by Peggy Holmes. Meanwhile, Sam has found a small apartment of her own and a job at a flower shop. As we come to know Sam better, we begin to understand that she feels alone, and is struggling to find her place in the world. But we also soon learn that Sam is resilient and optimistic, vivacious and considerate. What is making her life difficult on a daily basis is that she is plagued by bad luck. Put another way, some might say that Sam is a klutz. This is revealed through a number of funny scenes showing how she loses things, creates a mess wherever she goes, locks herself out of her bathroom, is often late for work, and even drops her morning toast, jam covered, face down. And so we find Sam sitting on a curb eating a sandwich, when a black cat comes and sits next to her and she offers it some of her Panini bread. articles.text: Sixth giraffe is added to the herd A new male giraffe was recently added to Oakland Zoo’s herd after traveling from Louisiana’s Audubon Nature Institute. He traveled in a carrier specially designed for the nearly 10-foot tall giraffe to ride comfortably. The 13-month-old giraffe was brought to the Zoo upon recommendation by the Association of Zoos and Aquariums’ (AZA) Species Survival Plan (SSP). The Animal Care team at Oakland Zoo has been working hard to ensure the area is comfortable for the new arrival, keeping his overall wellbeing in mind. Providing different options of enrichment, bedding, and tree browse gives the keepers a better understanding of his preferences and allows the giraffe to choose how he would like to interact with his new environment. While exploring his space, he discovered a bamboo wind chime made by his keepers and has since become enamored. “He is a brave and bold giraffe who’s adjusting quite well. We’re thrilled to get to know him and watch him develop a bond with his new herd at the Zoo,” said Amy Phelps, Oakland Zoo’s Zoological Manager. While he adjusts to his new home, he will have the opportunity to start getting to know his herd mates through a fence. articles.text: This recipe has been on repeat lately at our house and will fit right in with your May menu close to Cinco de Mayo. Fortunately, Mexican grocers are nearby so sourcing Oaxacan string cheese and tomatillos is doable. It’s fine to use another mild, melty cheese, and any salsa you enjoy. Just be aware the star of the show is the mushroom, so select complimentary, not competing, flavors. Tan bueno! Hen of the Woods Quesadillas with Avocado Salsa Makes 6 small quesadillas plus about 1 cup of salsa a few minutes. Char the tomatillos, jalapeno pepper, wedge of white onion and clove of garlic on as many sides as possible to a deep mahogany color. Remove to a plate as needed. Peel the charred skin from the jalapeno pepper using the back of a knife, or with your fingers, wearing gloves to protect your skin. Slice in half lengthwise to remove the stem, seeds and any stringy membrane. Slice into thin, julienne strips. Chop the avocado, tomatillos and onion into half inch pieces and add to a small food processor or blender. Add the garlic, cilantro and lime juice, salt and pepper. Blitz to form a smooth consistency. (If you have a molcajete use it!) Taste and add jalapeno, salt and/or pepper as desired. Transfer to a serving bowl, cover and set aside. Quesadillas Unravel the ball of Oaxacan string cheese and break off in 2-inch long pieces. Pull into shreds about 1/ 4-inch thick. Heat a large skillet over medium heat. Add the tablespoon of oil, then the clumps of mushrooms and sauté until lightly browned. Add the chopped garlic and continue cooking until the garlic just softens. Remove from the skillet and set aside. Place three tortillas onto the heated skillet (or comal) in a single layer and warm one side of each until softened and pliable. Flip each tortilla over and place one-sixth of the mushrooms, about two tablespoons of shredded cheese and a few strips of jalapeno pepper onto each tortilla. Move the filling to cover half of the tortilla so you can fold the remaining half over the filling. Cook until the first side turns golden brown then turn over to brown the remaining side. This should be sufficient to melt the cheese. Remove the cooked quesadillas to a plate and repeat cooking the remaining three quesadillas. Serve immediately with avocado salsa. For additional information and to search more recipes, see the blog of Piedmont resident Deborah Quok: https://www. piedmontpantry.com/.

articles.text: Saul Dan Timens, a longtime resident of Piedmont, passed away on May 6, 2024, at age 86. Saul was born and raised in Cleveland, Ohio and graduated from Cleveland Heights High School in 1954. Saul’s claim to fame was growing 10 inches during his freshman year. He loved to tell people that his friends used to visit him and “watch me grow.” In his youth, Saul worked during the summer as a driver for a Good Humor truck. Saul credits this job as the start of his lifelong love of ice cream. His favorite dessert for decades was the “Black and Tan” sundae at Fenton’s Creamery in Oakland. In 1958, Saul graduated Magna Cum Laude from Ohio University with a bachelor’s degree in business. He was president of Beta Gamma Sigma, the commerce honor fraternity, and a member of the Alpha Delta Chapter of Phi Sigma Delta. Saul served as an Officer in the Navy from 1958- 1961, assigned to USS Lookout, AGR2, a radar picket ship. He was proud of his service, saying it was instrumental in his growth as a person and a professional. Saul was a commercial property manager in the San Francisco Bay Area. He began his career at Coldwell Banker in Oakland before forming his own company, S D Timens and Company in 1981. He ran his own successful boutique firm until retiring in 2000. Saul lived most of his life in Oakland, Piedmont and Truckee. Saul enjoyed traveling in the Saul Timens passed away on May 6, 2024. He was 86. U.S. and abroad. He and Barbara enjoyed trips to Europe, Africa, Asia and Central America. In his later years, he took up oil painting, producing dozens and dozens of landscapes. Saul loved a good pun. He never failed to say, “I would relish some relish” every time the family had hot dogs instead of asking someone to pass along the condiment. Saul is predeceased by his parents Irving and Mildren Timens, and sister Annette Bedford. He is survived by his loving wife Barbara Bysiek Timens and daughter Laura Shipp, her husband Will Shipp and their children Claire and Olivia. He will also be missed by his stepchildren Paul and Beth Fischer and their children, Evie and Charlie. The family is planning a Celebration of Life on June 5th. In lieu of flowers, please consider donating to American Heart Association, or your favorite charity in Saul’s name. articles.text: The First Mondays Reading Group enjoyed a large turnout of 17 readers at their May 6 meeting outside the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park. The readers were there to discuss Perestroika in Paris, a 2020 fiction written by Jane Smiley. A review by the Wall Street Journal praised the novel as a successful combination of “the Parisian fairy tale and the equestrian novel.” The Journal also said, “Wholesomely timeless, full of good intentions and happy endings that feel far removed from the problems of the moment.” The New York Times called it a “feel-good escape.” Paras, short for Perestroika, is a spirited racehorse at a racetrack near Paris. articles.text: Last Wednesday, May 8, in advance of Mother’s Day was time for the Walking on Wednesdays group to make their annual visit to the Morcom Rose Garden on Jean Street in Oakland at the Piedmont city border. A big turnout of 45 walkers and four K-9 best friends showed up to see the garden. Meghan Bennett had created a website for the garden (https:// www.oaklandrose.com), so the walkers had lots of information. It is in a natural bowl on a 7.5- acre site that was purchased by the City of Oakland in 1911 and originally named Linda Vista Park. Local Oakland residents had petitioned and promised to contribute $8,000 for it. However, the best park entrance was through land in Piedmont. The Piedmont City Council joined the effort in June 1911 by acquiring Piedmont lots at the southern corner of Olive and Oakland Avenues to provide a “handsome entrance.” In 1913, it was proposed the park be converted into a zoological garden, but the park directors decided not to do it. The park’s conversion to a rose garden was a project of the Oakland Businessmen’s Garden Club in 1930 with the support of the city. It was originally known as the Municipal Rose Garden. Work began on the garden and the first first rose was planted on Jan. 27, 1933. The garden officially opened on May 28, 1933. The park’s name was changed in 1954 to honor former Oakland Mayor Fred Morcom, who served from 1931 to 1933. The park has been refurbished at least twice, in the 1950s and again in the 1990s, with many of the old roses, some going back to the 19th century, being regrafted on new rootstock. The group headed off down Magnolia to Wildwood Avenue and crossed Grand Avenue, which was originally called Pleasant Valley Road. A group photo was taken in front of the classical, curved colonnade entrance to the rose garden. A city employee said dogs on leashes were OK, so the group remained intact. The garden’s design was inspired by those of Italy and the park has over 2,400 rose bushes in three sections. There are winding walkways with a reflecting pool across from a 14-step cascade that goes down the hillside to the west and an octagonal wedding terrace above with more rose beds. The essential design has changed very little in the 90 years since it was created. What has changed is the City of Oakland’s ability to care for it. In the early 2000s, the hours of Oakland city workers to maintain the garden were reduced. A group of volunteers, the “Dedicated Deadheaders,” was organized to keep the garden beautiful, and they work there every Wednesday. In the early 2000s, “The Mother’s Walk” was created above the reflecting pool up to a Florentine oval garden at the north end of the park. There are brass plaques in the walkway with names of women honored each year in an annual ceremony on Mother’s Day. Walkers splintered off to see different sections of the garden. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are welcome. Register at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. pages.text: Wednesday, May 15, 2024 29 By Samantha Pell Piedmont Scouts eagerly anticipate the Camporee, an annual inter-troop campout once a year, often the first trip for new Scouts. This year they were met with 2024 Scout Camporee flushed out innumerable difficult circumstances, especially the weather, on the long-planned overnight campout. However, with true Scout spirit, they managed to make the best of it while learning some important life lessons. When Scouts piled into their carpools on the morning of May 4, many were brimming with excitement. Packs were stuffed with camping gear and no one had a clue about the theatrics that were to come. While they Scouts trudge through lush foliage. Scouts begin hiking up a hill, already wearing raincoats. As they neared Henry Coe State Park in Morgan Hill (Santa Clara County), rain began to seep through the clouds, slightly tarnishing their spirits. Luckily, the majority of Scouts had come prepared, protected by rain pants, windbreakers and the hope that the rain would let up soon. To the disappointment of many, the rain showed no signs of letting up and continued to pour down steadily, accompanied by sweeping gusts of wind. Troop 11 had decided to merely do a day hike and began hiking around 1 p.m. The other four troops persevered, holding onto hope. Members of the camporee staff held an emergency meeting and concluded that the safest option for all Scouts and adults was to hike out with the gear they could carry and effectively cancel camporee. While not the most popular choice, it was ultimately the most practical solution. After taking over the visitor center, Scouts climbed into vehicles with the heat on full blast and headed back to civilization. On Sunday, the “clean up crew” of Scouts on camp staff assembled at Piedmont Community Church – feeling rather refreshed from a good night’s sleep and comfortable mattresses – then returned to Henry Coe Park again. Due to the wet roads, Scouts had to hike in. Once at camp, the staff gorged themselves on the abandoned cold cuts and sandwich ingredients from the day before, savoring some belated sunshine. The next few hours were a flurry of activity as the staff gathered gear, aired out rain flies and even partook in a camporee activity - the team ski. In the long run – or rather, long hike – this rainsoaked, cancelled camporee held some of the most valuable lessons for young Scouts. One point of the Scout law that was incredibly useful for Scouts to hold on this trip was the eighth point: A Scout is cheerful. Quite frankly, while the trip was rather miserable at some points, when your umbrella had flipped out and rain is pelting on your cold head, being cheerful is difficult. Simply smiling and keeping calm put a positive spin on things for the Scouts, especially the younger Scouts. They remained upbeat for the majority of the hike. We can always keep smiling through freezing temperatures, through tough hikes, and through life. Just lift your head a little higher and remain...cheerful.
